text: Αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι αὐτῶν λυμαίνεται. Unum secundum substantiam animæ et corporis, ipsum eorum esse corrumpit: sic unitorum, quod ut sint unum, una essentia ac substantia, una in alterum demutanda sit, aut ambæ in tertiam: qui ipsorum interitus et ἀνυπαρξία. Turr. nihil Maximum expressit, ejusque vim omnem argumenti elisit. Ac indicasse sufficit.
anchorLine: αὐτὸ τὸ εἶναι αὐτῶν λυμαίνεται (k), εἰς ἀνυπαρξίαν
en: "Their very being is destroyed." The one according to the substance of soul and body corrupts their very being: so with things united, that they may be one, one essence and substance, one must be changed into the other, or both into a third: whose destruction is also non-existence. Turrianus expressed nothing of Maximus's point and removed the whole force of the argument. It suffices to have indicated this. (Print of 'Ac indicasse' is smeared; 'Ac' as read.)

text: Ταύτης γάρ. Hujus σχετικῆς unitionis unitio, una operatio, sive afflatus; quo Nestoriani singulariter agi Christum hominem a Verbo asserebant, more scilicet aliorum sanctorum, etsi quadam excellentia ob majorem puritatem, præ illis. Alii ὡς ἕνωσις: quasi in ea, quæ unitionis vice est, una operatio ac afflatus; quæ et ipsa subtilis Nestoriani dogmatis expressio est.
anchorLine: ῥιος, λέγειν ἕνωσιν· ταύτης γὰρ (l) ἡ μία ἐνέργεια
en: "For of this." Of this relational union, the union is one operation, or afflatus, by which the Nestorians asserted that the man Christ was moved singly by the Word, in the manner of other saints, though with a certain excellence because of greater purity, above them. Others read "as a union": as though in that which stands in the place of the union there were one operation and afflatus; which too is itself a subtle expression of the Nestorian doctrine.

text: Marg. Fr. Τὴν ἀναπλασθεῖσαν αὐτοῖς μίαν ἐνέργειαν· οὐ πρὸς τὸ ἔργον ἀπιδόντες, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὸν λόγον τῶν ἑνωθεισῶν οὐσιῶν ἀναπλάσαντες ταύτην· ἣν ὁ μέγας τραγέλαφον ἐκάλεσεν ἐνέργειαν, ὡς ἐπινοηματικὴν καὶ ἀνύπαρκτον· Fictam ab eis unam operationem, non ad opus respiciendo, sed ad rationem unitarum substantiarum, eam confingentes; vir magnus hircocervum vocarit, ut rationis figmentum, ac quod exsistentia careat et nihil sit.
anchorLine: ⁹⁰ Ὁπόταν οὐδὲ πρὸς ἔργον ἀντιδόντες, τὴν ἀνα-
en: Marginal reading (Fr.): "The one operation fashioned by them: not looking to the work, but fashioning it in view of the principle of the united substances; which the great man called a hircocervus (goat-stag) operation, as a figment of thought and non-existent." Latin: Fictam by them is one operation, not by looking to the work but to the principle of the united substances, they feigning it; the great man called it a hircocervus, as a figment of reason, and that which lacks existence and is nothing.

text: Ἀκραιφνεῖ ἑνώσει. Vera unitione, quam φυσικὴν et οὐσιώδη Cyrillus perinde dicit; distinctione ab ea quæ est σχετική. Ἄκρα occurrit Turriano cum reddit, propter summam cum ea unionem; quam vocem Patres Nestorio opponunt, ea potissimum ratione, ut significent primo statim ortu unitam carnem Verbo, ea unitione quæ est secundum hypostasim, non ex profectu, ut divino afflatu sic eximie donaretur, supra omnes prophetas consecutum esse.
anchorLine: τῇ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἀκραιφνεῖ ἑνώσει (n). Δι᾽ ἀμφοτέρων
en: "By pure union." By true union, which Cyrillus likewise calls natural and essential, as distinct from that which is relational. Turrianus has "akra" where he renders "on account of the highest union with it"; the Fathers set this word against Nestorius chiefly for the reason that they might signify that from the very first moment of origin the flesh was united to the Word, by the union which is according to hypostasis, not by progress, as if it were so exceptionally endowed with divine afflatus as to have attained a place above all the prophets.
note: print: Ἄκρα read as printed form of the word; 'donaretur' printed 'donarctur' (worn e)
